title-group.article-title: Predictive modeling of millet growth in pesticide- and vinasse-amended soils using SHAP regression interpretation

abstract.p: Soil contamination by persistent agrochemicals such as tebuthiuron (TB) and thiamethoxam (TX), together with the use of agroindustrial by-products like vinasse (VN), affects soil-plant interactions and crop development. This study evaluated the biometric responses of Pennisetum glaucum grown by measuring root and shoot dry biomass and leaf chlorophyll index in soils treated with combinations of TB, TX, and VN under controlled greenhouse conditions. Nine regression models were tested to predict plant responses based on these variables, considering or not plant development time, and interpreted using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP). The Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) and Random Forest (RF) models achieved the highest predictive performance (R² up to 0.27), whereas model accuracy declined sharply (R² < 0.05) when time was excluded, confirming its critical influence on predictive reliability. Vinasse improved plant growth, while TB and TX exerted neutral or negative effects, reflecting their persistence and potential phytotoxicity. These findings demonstrate the capacity of interpretable machine learning to elucidate soil-plant-contaminant interactions and support the design of sustainable management strategies for pesticide-impacted agricultural soils.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Soil contamination by pesticides and their residual concentrations is one of the foremost environmental challenges associated with modern agriculture, particularly in intensive cropping systems such as sugarcane production. Compounds like tebuthiuron, a substituted urea herbicide, and thiamethoxam, a neonicotinoid insecticide, are widely used for weed and pest control, respectively. These substances are characterized by their chemical persistence in the environment, variable soil mobility, and potential toxicity to non-target organisms, including soil microorganisms, edaphic fauna, and cultivated plants1,2. The detrimental effects of pesticide contamination manifest through the reduction of microbial biodiversity and the disruption of biochemical processes essential for soil fertility, such as nutrient cycling and structure maintenance, which impair the productivity of subsequent crops3. Thus, understanding the environmental behavior of these compounds and their interactions with soil components is essential for mitigating their cumulative ecological impacts.

In parallel, the application of agroindustrial by-products such as vinasse can alter soil physicochemical properties, influencing the bioavailability and fate of these pesticides, thus exacerbating environmental impacts2. Hence, although it is rich in organic matter and mineral components favorable to the crop4, the fertigation technique with vinasse or the use of bioinputs can alter the environmental behavior of pesticides, such as mobility and sorption rate (Kd), depending on the soil characteristics related to: pesticides association, organic matter, granulometry and classification, organic-mineral interactions, rainfall, and persistence5–8. This dual behavior reinforces the need to evaluate its combined effects with agrochemicals under realistic soil conditions.

In response to these challenges, species such as pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum), a summer annual forage grass which is useful for grazing, silage, hay, and green chop9. Exhibit significant root biomass production10, has ability to withstand drought, high pH, and heat stress9, plus has high tolerance to herbicide persistence in soil11, making them promising candidates for remediation strategies to mitigate these adverse consequences by pesticides and their intermediate degradation compounds.

Assessing the biometric responses of these plants under varying contamination levels requires analytical approaches capable of capturing the complexity and heterogeneity of experimental data. Traditional methods often fall short when confronted with the multidimensionality and non-linearity inherent to biological processes. Consequently, machine learning (ML) models have emerged as powerful tools for data analysis and prediction in ecology and agronomy12,13. Techniques such as random forest regression, support vector regression, and artificial neural networks (ANN) have been successfully applied to model plant responses to environmental pesticide contamination, identify key predictive variables, and forecast plant performance under diverse conditions14. For example, Ali et al.15 utilized ANN to model physiological responses of crops exposed to stress, highlighting these models’ capacity to handle complex interactions and noisy data.

Integrating machine learning with SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) introduces an interpretable framework for quantifying each variable’s contribution to plant development. This combination supports accurate prediction and transparent understanding of the processes underlying soil contamination and plant responses. Therefore, applying ML + SHAP to analyze soil-plant-contaminant interactions represent an innovative approach to disentangle complex non-linear relationships and to support sustainable management strategies for pesticide-impacted agricultural systems.

Therefore, this study aimed to apply and compare various ML regression models to describe the biometric responses of Pennisetum glaucum cultivated in soils contaminated with tebuthiuron, thiamethoxam and vinasse. By integrating advanced data analysis techniques with sustainable approaches, the results seek to contribute to the development of more effective and environmentally responsible strategies for managing contaminated soils in intensive agricultural systems.

sec.title: Location and material
sec.p: The experiment was performed under greenhouse conditions from January to May 2023 at 21°28′57″ S and 51°31′58″ W – Dracena, Brazil. The temperature and air humidity averages were 23.6 °C and 87%, respectively.

The soil (Utisol) collected until 0.20 m from Dracena (Brazil) presented 79.5% sand, 14.0% clay, and 6.5% silt. According to the soil characteristics in Table S1, the parameters for plant development were corrected by applying lime to increase the sum of bases until it reached 70%16.

The herbicide tebuthiuron was used as Combine® 500 SC (Dow AgroSciences – 1000 g ha−1 active ingredient [a.i.]) and the insecticide thiamethoxam as Actara® 750SG (Syngenta Crop Protection – 330 g ha−1 a.i.). Vinasse was obtained from a sugarcane energy plant at Dracena, Brazil. Finally, the seeds of Pennisetum glaucum were BRS 1501 from Embrapa – Brazil, commercially purchased from BRSEEDS Sementes® (75% germination rate and 95% purity).

sec.title: Experimental design
sec.p: Pesticides dosages followed the manufacturer’s leaflet according to the recommendations for the soil characteristics. The recommended volume of vinasse followed the regulations commonly used in sugarcane crops for a cost-effective chemical suppression of weeds and environmentally secure fertigation17.

Thus, the experimental design used 4.0 L pots for 16 tests with four replications each based on the presence or absence of: thiamethoxam (TX), tebuthiuron (TB), vinasse (VN), and pearl millet (P. glaucum) cultivation (Table 2).

Pesticides application was via a laboratorial device, which provided a suite of XR 11,002 flat nozzles every 0.5 m over a 1.0 m bar for broadcast spraying. A configurated sprayer released pesticides at 200 kPa, 0.65 L min−1, 5 km·h−1 and 0.75 m high from the top of the pots.

Vinasse was applied manually and uniformly the following day to simulate fertigation. Seven days later, Pennisetum glaucum seeds were sown into the pots (3.0 g per experimental unit). On the 10th day after sowing (10 DAS), seedlings were thinned to promote the growth of a single healthy individual. All experimental units received daily irrigation via automatic micro-sprinklers at 6 mm h⁻¹ for 1 h, ensuring adequate water supply for plant development.

caption.p: Factorial tests on the composition of soil samples.

sec.title: Monitoring plant development
sec.p: Several parameters monitored the growth of P. glaucum to assess the physiological responses of the plants to different soil samples until 60 DAS. Chlorophyll content in the leaves was determined using a portable chlorophyll meter in 20 and 60 DAS (ClorofiLOG® model CFL 1030, Falker), which provides rapid and non-destructive measures. It allows a real-time assessment of chlorophyll levels and enables accurate monitoring of plant physiological status under varying conditions.

Fresh and dry biomass were quantified to evaluate plant growth in 20 and 60 DAS. After completing all other measurements, shoot and root parts were weighed to determine fresh biomass. These samples were then dried in a forced-air oven at 65 °C for 72 h and reweighed to obtain dry biomass. This rigorous protocol provided detailed insights into how the different treatments, such as pesticide exposure and/or vinasse application, affected plant growth.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Dry mass (root and shoot) and chlorophyll index were modelled against TB, TX, and VN, with and without time as a longitudinal dimension. Response variables were scaled to [0, 1] through min-max normalization to reduce scale bias. Data were randomly split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets, repeated across 50 bootstrapped samples to assess stability and generalizability. A set of predictive techniques was applied to capture linear and non-linear relationships: lm, lasso, ridge, ctree, rf, gbm, xgb, svm, and gpr. Hyperparameters were kept consistent and conservative to minimise overfitting and ensure performance differences reflected model structure rather than tuning artefacts. Modelling followed established workflows, with full methodological details available in Kuhn & Johnson18. Performance was evaluated on test sets based on RMSE, MAE, and R², which are standard metrics for predictive accuracy and error dispersion in biological systems. To ensure interpretability, global and local SHAP values were computed on test data to prevent leakage19,20, while addressing transparency and reproducibility concerns. Analyses were conducted in R (v4.3.3) with the caret, mlr, and ggplot2 packages.

sec.title: Research involving plants
sec.p: The experimental research was carried out in accordance with the relevant institutional, national and international guidelines and legislation and, still, does not involve an endangered species. The seedlings of Pennisetum glaucum were commercially purchased, and the identification of these species was presented in accordance with Brazilian legislation.

sec.title: Results and discussion
sec.p: Figure 1 presents the regression prediction for root dry biomass, influenced or not by the plant’s development time.

caption.p: Regression performance of nine machine learning algorithms (ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb) for predicting Pennisetum glaucum root dry biomass (top) considering plant development time and (bottom) excluding plant development time. *Scatter plots with trend lines (in red) representing the relationship between observed and predicted values from different regression models: ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb. Each point corresponds to an individual prediction from one of the 50 datasets. RMSE, MAE, and R² metrics are indicated in each panel.

sec.p: The coefficients of determination (R²) were low across all tested models, indicating that development time alone was not sufficient to explain the observed variability in root dry biomass. The “gpr” model showed the best performance in terms of variance explanation (0.146), followed by “lm” (0.129) and “ridge” (0.128). The “rf” model (0.124) stood out for presenting the lowest mean absolute error (MAE 1055.841), suggesting good point accuracy.

On the other hand, “svm” model yielded the lowest MAE (879.803) but with a markedly low R² (0.050), which highlight its limitation in capturing broader trends within the dataset. Models such as “gbm” and “xgb” exhibited the worst performance (R² 0.046 and 0.036, respectively) and high error rates, indicating low predictive power under these experimental conditions.

Despite the application of machine learning techniques, these results indicate that the models’ ability to predict P. glaucum root dry biomass overtime in soil was limited. No model achieved a coefficient of determination above 0.15, demonstrating that the factor time alone is not a sufficient predictor to capture the complexity of the plant physiological responses to tebuthiuron, thiamethoxam, and/or vinasse.

The superior performance of “gpr” and “rf” models may be attributed to their ability to handle non-linear data and irregular distributions21–23, typical characteristics of experiments involving multiple environmental stress factors. In particular, “gpr” incorporates uncertainties associated with predictions and shows a promising approach for scenarios with high data noise21.

Figure 2 presents the SHAP model for improved interpretability of the most important variable influencing root dry biomass. Time became the dominant predictive factor, showing the highest and most widely distributed SHAP values across the models. In contrast, pesticides maintained a secondary influence, suggesting a possible cumulative or delayed residual effect as observed by Ferreira et al.2, who studied the residual activity and sorption of tebuthiuron in different soils. These authors observed that residual activity of this herbicide decreases overtime, with no toxicity detected 360 days after application in soil, but higher sorption occurs with higher organic carbon and clay contents, as the vinasse addition in this study. The presence of this agroindustrial residue promoted a relevance as a predictive variable, although with less relative importance compared to time, possibly due to its role as a soil conditioner rather than a direct toxic contaminant.

Thus, the interaction between the compounds probably affects nutrient availability, microbial activity, and root absorption, resulting in plant growth variations that are not easily explained by time alone. Previous studies have shown that herbicides such as tebuthiuron exhibit high persistence in soil and can compromise the root system of non-target plants for extended periods, which may explain the variability observed in root dry biomass24. Similarly, vinasse can act as a soil conditioner25 or, depending on the dose, as a source of stress7.

However, when “plant development time” was removed from the regression models for root dry biomass (Fig. 1b), an even greater decline in the predictive performance of the algorithms was observed. No model exceeded 0.022 for the coefficient of determination, which indicate an almost negligible explanation of the variability for P. glaucum root dry biomass.

Although extremely low, “lm” (0.022), “ridge” (0.022), and “lasso” (0.012) yielded the highest R² values, with RMSE ranging from 2875 to 2890 g/plant. These results suggest a slight advantage of these models in detecting minimal patterns in the data. In contrast, “rf”, “gpr” and “xgb” showed values between zero and 0.008 and confirmed their limited modeling capacity. Even the “rf” model, which presented a relatively higher MAE (1338.5 g), failed to explain the variance in the data. The “svm” model achieved the lowest MAE (924.92 g), but with a null R² that reinforce its predictions may be centered around the mean without capturing actual variations. Finally, “gbm” was the least suitable model in terms of absolute error (MAE 2062.6 g) with a negligible R² (0.005), indicating its inadequacy for the data pattern.

The absence of time as a predictor variable substantially compromised the statistical model’s performance. This is expected as time is directly associated with the dynamics of root growth26. Therefore, ignoring this factor implies if all plant development stages equally impact root dry biomass, which is biologically inaccurate.

Furthermore, the compounds applied in soil (TB, TX, and VN) affect P. glaucum in dynamic and cumulative ways, with their effects varying according to exposure time, phenological stage, and chemical stress intensity. Therefore, excluding time removes an essential component in explaining the plant’s response to the environment.

The distribution of SHAP values was concentrated and showed low variability among the applied residues when the time variable was excluded (Fig. 2). Although vinasse exhibited a higher relative contribution in most models, the effects of tebuthiuron and thiamethoxam were also relevant in models, such as “rf” and “xgb”. However, the low amplitude of SHAP values confirms the limited predictive influence of these variables when isolated from the time factor.

caption.p: SHAP values for predicting root dry biomass of Pennisetum glaucum (top) considering plant development time or (bottom) excluding plant development time. Boxplots with colored scatter display the SHAP values assigned across different models to each explanatory variable: VN (vinasse), TX (thiamethoxam), time, and TB (tebuthiuron). The colors represent the magnitude of the original feature values from different regression models: ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb.

sec.p: In relation to the predictive analysis of shoot dry biomass of P. glaucum, significant variations in performance among the tested regression models were shown under the influence of development time or excluding plant development time (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Regression performance of nine machine learning algorithms (ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb) for predicting Pennisetum glaucum shoot dry biomass (top) considering plant development time or (bottom) excluding plant development time. *Scatter plots with trend lines (in red) representing the relationship between observed and predicted values from different regression models: ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb. Each point corresponds to an individual prediction from one of the 50 datasets. RMSE, MAE, and R² metrics are indicated in each panel.

sec.p: Among the algorithms evaluated, “gpr” demonstrated the best overall performance (R² 0.268, RMSE 2657.95, MAE 1410.60), which suggest a relatively superior ability to capture response variability as a function of the predictors. The “rf” and “lm” models also show a satisfactory performance compared to the other algorithms (R² 0.222 and 0.194, respectively). The penalized linear models “lasso” (0.187) and “ridge” (0.1963) demonstrated similar performances, emphasizing that plant development time slightly improved the performance of these methods. Although commonly used for their reliability in regression tasks27, “gbm” (0.077) and “xgb” (0.09) showed weaker performance, with RMSE values exceeding 2900. The “svm” model, despite achieving the lowest MAE (1076.97), demonstrated limited explanatory power (0.191), suggesting predictions close to the overall mean but with low variance explained.

Hence, time inclusion as an explanatory variable contributed to improve model fitting, as evidenced by the overall increase in coefficients of determination compared to the evaluation without it. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the models’ ability to represent shoot biomass growth is directly related to the complexity of interactions between the pesticides and the soil environment overtime.

Therefore, plant development time had the greatest positive impact on shoot dry biomass prediction, particularly in “lasso”, “ridge”, “lm”, and “gpr”. The SHAP values associated with time in these models (Fig. 4) showed a broader distribution centered around positive values, indicating that longer cultivation periods were consistently linked to greater shoot biomass.

Vinasse presence also showed considerable importance, with positive effects in the “lm”, “lasso”, “ridge” and “gbm” models, suggesting that its presence may have contributed to greater nutrient availability and, consequently, promoted shoot growth. Similar findings were reported by Ferreira et al.25, who observed that vinasse contributed to biomass development of Pennisetum glaucum and Mucuna pruriens in soil containing tebuthiuron.

The pesticides exhibited varied effects generally associated with SHAP values that were negative or showed minimal positive contribution across the statistical models. Tebuthiuron presented SHAP values concentrated near zero or negative for “xgb”, “lm”, “lasso” and “gpr”, which indicate its inhibitory or negligible effect on shoot biomass. Although showing some variability, thiamethoxam had a more discreet and less consistent contribution among the models.

It is important to highlight that the best-performing predictive models “gpr” and “rf” that captured the combined influence of time, tebuthiuron and vinasse. These algorithms visually demonstrated a clear pattern of separation among SHAP values and indicated greater sensitivity to the complex interactions between soil factors and plant development.

Thus, the SHAP analysis results endorse the hypothesis that plant development time is the primary determinant of P. glaucum shoot biomass in soils containing the organic residue and pesticides, followed by vinasse presence as a potentially growth-promoting factor, while tebuthiuron and thiamethoxam applications tended to exert negative or neutral effects on the response variable.

Results without including plant development time as a predictor demonstrated a limited predictive performance across all models with R² values below 0.04. Thus, it was expressed a variability less than 4% for dry biomass that was explained by the isolated environmental variables. The “ridge” model showed the best performance (RMSE 2984.93; MAE 1631.82; R² 0.035), followed by the “lm” (RMSE 2978.44; R² 0.034). Nevertheless, these values indicate low predictive accuracy, suggesting that the included factors, although relevant, are insufficient to explain the complexity of accumulated shoot biomass.

In this way, P. glaucum shoot dry biomass cannot be adequately explained solely by VN, TB, and TX excluding plant development time. The absence of time compromises the modeling of the physiological process of plant growth, which is inherently dynamic. Accordingly, SHAP analysis provided explanations on the individual contribution of each variable in the predictive models (Fig. 4).

Overall, tebuthiuron showed the greatest negative influence on dry biomass in the most responsive models. For “rf”, “gbm” and “xgb”, the herbicide presence exhibited a wider dispersion of SHAP values with negative intensity, indicating a more consistent deleterious effect on P. glaucum growth. Vinasse presence showed a predominantly positive contribution in several models (especially for “gbm”, “gpr” and “xgb”), supporting its potential role as a soil conditioner and fertilizer. Thiamethoxam demonstrated intermediate variation with a less pronounced impact compared to tebuthiuron and vinasse. In the linear models, the influence of all three factors was more subdued presenting a little variation in SHAP values, which infer their limitation in capturing complex interactions.
In addition to plant biomass, the leaf chlorophyll index of P. glaucum was evaluated, and its regression results influenced or not by plant development time are presented in Fig. 5.

Boxplots with colored scatter display the SHAP values assigned across different models to each explanatory variable: VN (vinasse), TX (thiamethoxam), time, and TB (tebuthiuron). The colors represent the magnitude of the original feature values from different regression models: ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb.

Regression performance of nine machine learning algorithms (ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb) for predicting Pennisetum glaucum leaf chlorophyll index considering (top) plant development time or (bottom) excluding plant development time. *Scatter plots with trend lines (in red) representing the relationship between observed and predicted values from different regression models: ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb. Each point corresponds to an individual prediction from one of the 50 datasets. RMSE, MAE, and R² metrics are indicated in each panel.

sec.p: The best performing model for leaf chlorophyll index was “svm” (RMSE 14.469; MAE 9.988; R² 0.032) that show a slight ability to capture patterns between the input variables and plant development time. The linear models (“lm”, “ridge”, “lasso”) also demonstrated similar performance, with RMSE and MAE values close to each other and low coefficients of determination (from 0.018 to 0.026), indicating low explained variability. Tree-based models (“ctree”, “rf”, “gbm”, “xgb”) did not outperform the linear models. The low R² observed for all models suggests that the tested factors have limited influence on the development time of P. glaucum.

The SHAP analysis (Fig. 6) for leaf chlorophyll index showed that no variable exhibited clear and consistent dominance and indicated the low explanatory power (low R²). However, the “gbm”, “rf” and “xgb” implied that all variables had modest and relatively balanced contributions to the prediction, with slight emphasis on tebuthiuron and vinasse. Additionally, “svm” model displayed greater dispersion with time and herbicide presence in soil appearing with slightly higher importance. In the linear models and “gpr”, SHAP values showed less variability. This result advised that these models assigned more consistent weights to all variables. Finally, “ctree” presented near-zero SHAP values for all variables, consistent with its previously observed poor predictive performance.

Finally, the last statistical analysis again considered the leaf chlorophyll index data, but with the exclusion of the plant development time as well as the biomass measurements (Fig. 5). All models exhibited extremely limited performance with R² values ranging from 0.000 to 0.004. These findings demonstrated that practically no variation in variable response could be explained. The ranges for RMSE (14.74–17.21) and MAE (10.088–12.40) suggested a high mean error rate in predictions.

Compared to the scenario where development time was included as an explanatory variable (Fig. 5), the models were slightly more effective despite modest R² values. Thus, the duration of exposure to inputs and the environment plays a fundamental role in crop response and acts as a mediator of physiological effects.

According to SHAP values for these data (Fig. 6), tebuthiuron showed the greatest variability, especially those models based on tree algorithms (“gbm”, “rf”, “xgb”), whose influence is more sensitive to context or interactions with other variables, even though its average contribution was not high. In some cases, the negative impact (SHAP values < 0) may indicate a possible inhibitory of herbicide effect on the variable response. Vinasse and thiamethoxam showed modest and relatively consistent positive contributions across most models, with less dispersion in SHAP values. Although presented low magnitudes near zero, “lm”, “lasso” and “ridge” highlighted both variables as slightly more relevant than tebuthiuron. For “xgb”, a wide dispersion of SHAP values was observed and tebuthiuron presented negative contributions at various points, which express possible toxicity at high concentrations. The “ctree” model once again showed virtually null SHAP values, corroborating its limited predictive capacity as previously indicated in the regression analysis.

Despite some differences among the models tested, no single variable proved dominant, and most SHAP values remained close to zero, indicating low explainability. These results complement the previous regression analysis, which also revealed low R² even for complex algorithms. Therefore, the absence of time as a predictive variable substantially reduces the models’ ability to capture system dynamics and emphasizes the hypothesis that soil treatment effects are modulated overtime or depend on interactions with variables not included in the models.

Boxplots with colored scatter display the SHAP values assigned across different models to each explanatory variable: VN (vinasse), TX (thiamethoxam), time, and TB (tebuthiuron). The colors represent the magnitude of the original feature values from different regression models: ctree, gbm, gpr, lasso, lm, rf, ridge, svm, xgb.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The phenological development time of Pennisetum glaucum is the primary determinant in predictive accuracy of biometric variables under soil with tebuthiuron, thiamethoxam and/or vinasse. Regression models combined with SHAP interpretation revealed that excluding the temporal variable substantially reduced the explanatory capacity of the algorithms. Thus, the factor “time” is crucial and directly infers the dynamic complexity of soil-plant-contaminant interactions. Therefore, these results underscore the importance of incorporating temporally sensitive predictive approaches into sustainable management strategies for soils impacted by persistent agrochemicals.

This study evaluated the performance and interpretability of various regression algorithms applied to uncertain and complex experimental datasets, rather than aiming for a detailed physiological or biochemical analysis of plant responses. The focus was on how machine learning models handle variability, noise, and nonlinearity. Among the tested algorithms, “gpr” and “rf” consistently achieved the highest predictive accuracy, reflecting their ability to capture nonlinear relationships and interactions among experimental factors. The models reproduced expected patterns, such as the positive effect of vinasse on plant growth and the neutral or inhibitory influence of tebuthiuron, demonstrating their capacity to extract coherent trends from noisy data despite biological interpretation not being the primary objective. These findings highlight the potential of interpretable machine learning to support predictive and sustainable approaches in environmental and soil science.
